items.prompt: Which expression tests whether zero-based bit k is set in x?

options.text: (x AND (1 shifted left by k)) is nonzero.
(x OR (1 shifted left by k)) is nonzero.
(x XOR (1 shifted left by k)) is zero.

feedback.reason: AND preserves the selected bit only when it is set in both x and the one-hot mask.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The selector 1 shifted left by k contains a one only at position k. AND clears every other position and leaves that selected one only if x also has a one there. Therefore x AND selector is either zero (bit k clear) or exactly the selector (bit k set). This observes the previous state without mutating x.

items: Validate 0 ≤ k < usable word width before shifting.
Build oneHot = 1 shifted left by k.
Evaluate (x AND oneHot) != 0 to obtain the membership predicate.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: For “all required” compare (x AND mask) with mask. For “at least one” compare the same expression with zero; these are different predicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.or_nonzero: OR forces bit k to one, so a nonzero result cannot distinguish whether that bit was previously clear.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.xor_zero: XOR produces a modified value and equals zero only under a much stronger whole-word equality condition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add_mask: Addition is arithmetic rather than a membership test and a carry can change positions above bit k.

items.prompt: Which operation sets every bit selected by mask without clearing unselected bits?

feedback.reason: OR forces selected positions to one and leaves every zero-mask position unchanged.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Check OR one position at a time. Where mask has one, x OR 1 is always one, so the selected position becomes set. Where mask has zero, x OR 0 equals x, so every unselected position is preserved. The same truth table applies whether mask selects one feature or several.

items: Selected position: 0 OR 1 = 1 and 1 OR 1 = 1.
Unselected position: 0 OR 0 = 0 and 1 OR 0 = 1.
Thus updated = x OR mask establishes all selected bits without disturbing the rest.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Clear uses AND with a width-limited complement: selected positions become 0 and all other positions see AND with 1. A raw complement without a width model can hide portability errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_mask: At every unselected position mask has zero, and x AND zero clears that position instead of preserving x.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.xor_mask: XOR with one flips a selected bit, so a bit that was already enabled would be disabled.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_not_mask: The complemented mask supplies zero at selected positions, making this the operation for clearing rather than setting.

items.prompt: Using a width-limited complement, which operation clears every bit selected by mask?

feedback.reason: Complement(mask) has zeros at selected positions and ones elsewhere within the declared width.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Within the declared width, complement(mask) swaps selected ones to zeros and unselected zeros to ones. AND with zero forces every selected position to zero; AND with one preserves each unselected bit from x. Limiting the complement to the word width keeps the reasoning independent of a language's sign extension or arbitrary-precision representation.

items: Normalize mask to the declared word width.
Complement those width-limited bits so selected positions become zero.
Compute x AND complementedMask; verify updated AND originalMask equals zero.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Clear uses AND with a width-limited complement: selected positions become 0 and all other positions see AND with 1. A raw complement without a width model can hide portability errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.or_mask: OR forces selected positions to one, which is the opposite of the required clear postcondition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.xor_mask: XOR flips selected positions, so an initially clear bit would become one instead of remaining zero.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_mask: Direct AND retains only selected positions and clears unselected ones, reversing which part should be preserved.

constraints: Complement is limited to the declared storage width.

items.prompt: Which operation toggles every bit selected by mask?

feedback.reason: XOR with one flips a bit, while XOR with zero preserves it.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

XOR's one-bit truth table matches toggle exactly: 0 XOR 1 = 1 and 1 XOR 1 = 0. At positions not selected by mask, XOR with zero leaves both possible input bits unchanged. Applying x XOR mask therefore inverts every selected position and preserves all others without branching per bit.

items: Mask one selects a position for inversion.
Mask zero acts as identity at an unselected position.
A second XOR with the same mask reverses the transition.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: XOR with 1 flips and XOR with 0 preserves. Applying the same mask twice restores the original word because m XOR m is zero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.or_mask: OR can change zero to one but leaves one as one, so it cannot implement both directions of a toggle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_mask: AND with one preserves a selected input bit rather than replacing it with its opposite value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_not_mask: AND with the complemented mask deterministically clears selected positions instead of inverting their prior values.

items.prompt: What happens if the same set operation x = x OR mask is applied twice?

options.text: The second application makes no additional change.
The selected bits are cleared by the second application.
The numeric value increases by mask again.

feedback.reason: Setting selected bits is idempotent.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

After the first update y = x OR mask, every one in mask is already present in y. Reapplying the operation gives y OR mask = (x OR mask) OR mask = x OR (mask OR mask) = x OR mask because a OR a = a. Unselected positions also remain unchanged because they are ORed with zero both times.

items: First OR establishes the postcondition that all mask positions are one.
Second OR applies one to positions already one and zero elsewhere.
The word after the second update is identical to the word after the first.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: XOR with 1 flips and XOR with 0 preserves. Applying the same mask twice restores the original word because m XOR m is zero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.toggles_off: OR with one always returns one, so repeating it cannot clear a selected bit as XOR would.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adds_mask: OR combines bit presence rather than adding numeric values, so an already-set mask contributes no second increase.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clears_others: At unselected positions the mask is zero, and x OR zero preserves the original bit on every application.

items.prompt: What happens if the same clear operation x = x AND complement(mask) is applied twice?

options.text: The second application makes no additional change.
The selected bits become one again.
The second application clears every bit.

feedback.reason: Clearing selected bits is idempotent.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Let c be the width-limited complement of mask. After one update y = x AND c, selected positions are zero and unselected positions equal x. A second update yields (x AND c) AND c = x AND (c AND c) = x AND c because a AND a = a. Nothing can restore the selected bits because both applications AND them with zero.

items: First clear makes every selected position zero.
Second clear again applies zero to selected positions and one elsewhere.
The postcondition and all unselected bits remain unchanged.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Clear uses AND with a width-limited complement: selected positions become 0 and all other positions see AND with 1. A raw complement without a width model can hide portability errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sets_again: The complemented mask still contains zero at every selected position, so no second application can set those bits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clears_all: Unselected positions meet one in the complemented mask and therefore preserve their previous values on both passes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.increments: Bitwise AND can only preserve or clear a one bit; it does not perform arithmetic addition.

constraints: Complement is limited to the declared storage width.

items.prompt: What is the effect of toggling the same mask twice?

feedback.reason: XOR is self-inverse for a fixed mask.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Associativity lets us regroup (x XOR mask) XOR mask as x XOR (mask XOR mask). Every bit XOR itself is zero, so mask XOR mask = 0; zero is XOR's identity, giving x XOR 0 = x. Per bit, a selected value flips twice while an unselected value is preserved twice.

items: First XOR inverts exactly the selected positions.
Second XOR inverts those same positions again.
Algebraically the two identical masks cancel, restoring the complete original word.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: XOR with 1 flips and XOR with 0 preserves. Applying the same mask twice restores the original word because m XOR m is zero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sets_mask: OR would force selected bits on; two XOR updates instead return each selected bit to its initial state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clears_mask: The result cannot be always clear because two inversions restore both initially clear and initially set bits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverses_bits: XOR changes values only at corresponding positions and never moves a bit to a different position.

items.prompt: Which expression tests whether all bits selected by mask are already set in x?

feedback.reason: AND extracts the selected positions from x.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The expression x AND mask removes all unselected positions and retains only selected positions that are actually set in x. If even one required bit is absent, the extracted result has zero where mask has one and cannot equal mask. Equality therefore proves every selected position is present. A nonzero comparison proves only that at least one survived.

items: Extract present required bits with x AND mask.
Use equality with mask for the universal condition 'all selected bits'.
Use nonzero only for the existential condition 'at least one selected bit'.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: For “all required” compare (x AND mask) with mask. For “at least one” compare the same expression with zero; these are different predicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_nonzero: One shared bit is enough to make AND nonzero, so other required positions may still be missing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.or_equals_zero: For any nonzero required mask, OR preserves its one bits and therefore cannot produce an all-zero result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.xor_equals_mask: XOR compares differences across positions; equality with mask does not isolate the universal selected-bit membership condition.

items.prompt: Which expression tests whether at least one bit selected by mask is set in x?

feedback.reason: Any shared one position survives AND and makes the result nonzero.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

AND produces one exactly at positions where both x and mask contain one. Therefore a nonzero result is a witness that at least one selected position overlaps x. The result need not equal mask: for mask 0110 and x 0010, the AND is 0010, which correctly proves overlap while also showing that not all selected bits are set.

items: Compute overlap = x AND mask.
Compare overlap with zero for the existential condition.
Compare overlap with mask only when the requirement changes to all selected positions.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: For “all required” compare (x AND mask) with mask. For “at least one” compare the same expression with zero; these are different predicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_equals_mask: Equality requires every one in mask to survive, which is stronger than finding at least one shared position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.or_equals_x: This also holds only when every selected mask bit is already present in x, not for partial overlap.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.xor_zero: A zero XOR result requires x and mask to match at every represented position, far beyond sharing one bit.

items.prompt: An 8-bit word is 10101100 and mask is 00001100. What is the result of clearing the selected mask bits?

feedback.reason: The mask selects bit positions 2 and 3, both of which become zero.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Within eight bits, complement(00001100) is 11110011. Clearing computes 10101100 AND 11110011. At positions 3 and 2, the complemented mask supplies zeros, so the existing ones are removed; at every other position it supplies one and preserves the source. The row-by-row result is 10100000.

items: Original:   10101100
Clear mask: 00001100; eight-bit complement: 11110011
AND result: 10100000

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Clear uses AND with a width-limited complement: selected positions become 0 and all other positions see AND with 1. A raw complement without a width model can hide portability errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bits_10101100: This leaves positions 2 and 3 set, so it fails the required postcondition that both selected bits become zero.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bits_00001100: This is x AND mask, which extracts the selected bits instead of preserving all unselected positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bits_10101111: This resembles setting low positions with OR and leaves the selected positions one rather than clearing them.

constraints: Use exactly 8 bits for complement and results.

items.prompt: Which identities are correct for a fixed-width word x and mask m? Select all that apply.

options.text: (x OR m) OR m equals x OR m.
(x AND complement(m)) AND complement(m) equals x AND complement(m).
(x XOR m) XOR m equals x.
(x XOR m) XOR m equals x XOR m.

feedback.reason: Set and clear are idempotent, while toggle is self-inverse.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

OR and AND are idempotent: repeating the same operand changes nothing after the first application, which proves both set and clear identities. XOR is different: identical masks cancel, so two toggles return x rather than preserve the once-toggled state. These laws apply position by position within the declared fixed width.

items: Accept `set_idempotent` because m OR m = m.
Accept `clear_idempotent` because complement(m) AND itself is unchanged.
Accept `toggle_twice` because m XOR m = 0.
Reject `toggle_idempotent` because the second toggle cancels the first.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Evaluate each candidate per bit. A zero in the mask is the identity for OR, XOR, and AND NOT, but ordinary AND would erase unselected bits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.toggle_idempotent: Two identical XOR masks cancel to zero, so the result is x rather than the once-toggled value x XOR m.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.set_idempotent: OR with the same mask is idempotent.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.clear_idempotent: Clearing the same positions twice has no extra effect.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.toggle_twice: XOR with the same mask cancels.

items.prompt: Which operations preserve every bit position where mask has zero? Select all that apply.

feedback.reason: A zero mask position should act as an identity at every unselected bit.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At an unselected position mask = 0. OR uses x OR 0 = x, XOR uses x XOR 0 = x, and clearing uses x AND complement(0) = x AND 1 = x. Direct AND is the exception: x AND 0 = 0, so it erases an unselected one. Evaluating the mask-zero row is enough to decide this preservation question.

items: Accept `or_mask`: zero is OR's identity.
Accept `xor_mask`: zero is XOR's identity.
Accept `and_not_mask`: complementing zero supplies AND's identity one.
Reject `and_mask`: AND with the mask's zero destroys an unselected one.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Evaluate each candidate per bit. A zero in the mask is the identity for OR, XOR, and AND NOT, but ordinary AND would erase unselected bits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.and_mask: At every unselected position mask is zero, and x AND zero forces the output to zero instead of preserving x.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.and_not_mask: The complemented mask contains ones at zero-mask positions.

items.prompt: Which statements about clearing with complement are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The complement must be interpreted within a declared width.
Clearing is equivalent to XOR for every initial word.

feedback.reason: Clear has a deterministic zero result at selected positions and identity elsewhere.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Clearing computes x AND a complemented mask. The complement must be interpreted in the same width as x so its selected positions are zero and all other represented positions are one. AND then forces selected bits to zero and preserves unselected bits. XOR cannot replace this operation: it turns an initially clear selected bit on, while clear must produce zero for both possible inputs.

items: Accept `width_matters`: complement has meaning only relative to represented positions.
Accept `selected_zero`: selected mask ones become complement zeros.
Accept `others_preserved`: unselected mask zeros become complement ones.
Reject `same_as_xor`: toggle depends on prior state instead of guaranteeing zero.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Clear uses AND with a width-limited complement: selected positions become 0 and all other positions see AND with 1. A raw complement without a width model can hide portability errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_as_xor: For a selected bit initially zero, XOR with one returns one while clear with complemented-mask AND returns zero.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.width_matters: High-bit behavior depends on the word boundary.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.selected_zero: The complemented mask has zeros there.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.others_preserved: The complemented mask has ones there.

items.prompt: Which operation choices match the stated requirement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use OR to enable one or more flags without disabling others.
Use AND with width-limited complement to disable selected flags.
Use XOR to invert selected flags.
Use a nonzero AND result to prove all required flags are enabled.

feedback.reason: The operation must match whether the contract requires one, zero, inversion, or observation.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Each requirement names a different selected-position postcondition. OR guarantees one, complemented-mask AND guarantees zero, and XOR guarantees inversion, while all preserve unselected positions. Observation needs a separate predicate: (state AND mask) = mask proves every required flag is set; merely comparing with zero proves only that one or more flags overlap.

items: Accept `enable_flags`: OR establishes one at every selected position.
Accept `disable_flags`: AND with the width-limited complement establishes zero.
Accept `flip_flags`: XOR inverts selected state.
Reject `check_all_with_nonzero`: it implements an at-least-one test.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Evaluate each candidate per bit. A zero in the mask is the identity for OR, XOR, and AND NOT, but ordinary AND would erase unselected bits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.check_all_with_nonzero: With mask 0110 and state 0010 the AND is nonzero although one required bit is missing, so it cannot prove all.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.enable_flags: OR forces selected bits to one.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for testing zero-based bit k.

elements.text: Confirm k is inside the declared word width.
Construct a one-hot mask with bit k set.
AND the word with the mask.
Treat a nonzero result as set and zero as clear.

feedback.reason: A bit test depends on a legal position and a one-hot selector.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Validity comes before the shift because an out-of-range k can overflow, wrap, or invoke language-specific behavior. Once k is valid, the one-hot mask identifies exactly one position. AND extracts that position from x, and only then can zero versus nonzero be interpreted as clear versus set.

items: Confirm that k is within the declared usable word width.
Construct oneHot = 1 shifted left by k.
Compute selected = x AND oneHot.
Interpret selected != 0 as set and selected = 0 as clear.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Do not build the selector before validating k. The later AND cannot repair a shift that already addressed an invalid position.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for setting a selected feature and verifying it.

elements.text: Build the feature's one-hot or multi-bit mask.
Update state with state OR mask.
Verify the extracted bits equal mask.

feedback.reason: OR applies the state transition, and equality verifies all selected bits.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The feature mapping first determines the one-hot or multi-bit mask. OR must update the state before the result is inspected. AND then extracts the selected positions from that updated state, and equality with the complete mask proves every required bit is one. Checking only for nonzero would accept a partial multi-bit update.

items: Build the feature mask from its declared bit positions.
Compute updatedState = state OR mask.
Extract present selected bits with updatedState AND mask.
Compare the extraction with mask to verify that all selected bits are enabled.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Verification belongs after the transition and must use equality for a multi-bit requirement; a pre-update or nonzero check proves a different claim.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for safely clearing a mask in an 8-bit word.

elements.text: AND the word with the complemented mask.
Verify word AND originalMask equals zero.

feedback.reason: The width-limited complement creates zeros only at selected positions.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The original mask must first be represented in exactly eight bits, because that defines which positions its complement may affect. Flipping those eight bits creates zeroes at selected positions and ones elsewhere. AND applies the clear transition. Testing the updated word against the original mask then proves no selected one remains.

items: Normalize the original mask to exactly eight represented bits.
Complement those eight bits.
Update word = word AND complementedMask.
Verify word AND originalMask = 0.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Keep the original mask for verification. Testing against the complemented mask would inspect preserved positions rather than prove that every selected position was cleared.

items.prompt: Arrange the reasoning for toggling a mask twice.

elements.text: Rewrite z as x XOR (mask XOR mask).
Use mask XOR mask = 0 and x XOR 0 = x.

feedback.reason: XOR associativity and self-cancellation prove that toggle is reversible.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The first update defines y as the once-toggled state. The second applies the identical mask to y. Substitution and associativity regroup the expression so the two masks are adjacent; self-cancellation reduces them to zero, and XOR's identity law then reduces the complete expression to x.

items: Compute y = x XOR mask.
Compute z = y XOR mask.
Substitute y and associate: z = x XOR (mask XOR mask).
Use mask XOR mask = 0 and x XOR 0 = x.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The cancellation requires the same mask on both updates. Different masks would leave their XOR difference applied to x.

items.prompt: On a fixed-width machine word, a function builds one mask and tests, sets, or clears one bit using a constant number of bitwise operations. Select time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: The word width is a fixed machine constant.
The shift count is within the valid width.

feedback.reason: Under the fixed-word model, each primitive bitwise operation is constant time.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The stated machine model treats shift, AND, OR, XOR and complement on one fixed-width word as primitive O(1) operations. Building one selector and applying a constant number c of those operations costs c · O(1) = O(1). The function retains only x, the selector and a constant number of scalar temporaries, so peak auxiliary space is also O(1).

items: Count a constant number of fixed-word primitives, independent of the numeric bit position.
Count a constant number of word-sized temporaries.
Do not transfer this bound to an arbitrary-precision integer whose width grows with input.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The fixed-width assumption is the boundary of the result. If the represented word grows to w bits, primitive cost may depend on w and must be analyzed under that representation.

items.prompt: A function applies q independently specified bit updates to one fixed-width word, using O(1) work per update. Select total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: The q update descriptions are provided as input.

feedback.reason: Constant-time primitive updates still accumulate linearly across q requested operations.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Each requested update performs O(1) fixed-word work, and all q independently specified updates must be processed. Summing the per-update costs gives q · O(1) = O(q) total time. The updates modify one running word and reuse a constant number of masks or temporaries, so peak auxiliary space remains O(1) rather than accumulating with q.

items: Per-update cost: O(1) under the fixed-word model.
Number of required updates: q, yielding total time O(q).
Peak retained working state: one word plus constant temporaries, yielding O(1) auxiliary space.

blocks.title: Cost model
blocks.text: O(1) describes one update, not the whole request. Space stays constant only because the function does not retain the q update history or q intermediate words.
